source.title: Small-to-Large Generalization: Data Influences Models Consistently Across Scale
source.authors: Alaa Khaddaj; Logan Engstrom; A. Ma̧dry

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure and table text is garbled or flattened, and the main text and Appendix B give different names/sizes for the small model used in Figure 1 (57M in the main text; MPT-80M in Appendix B).
record.tranche_reason: The study uses small proxy models and Chinchilla-optimal token-to-parameter ratios, but it does not fit or test the claimed loss power laws or compute-optimal allocation laws. Its own results compare loss correlations across changes in training data distributions.
record.gate_note: The reported small-to-large loss correlations concern how training-data changes affect model losses, not whether held-out loss follows a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute, or whether small-run power-law fits extrapolate. The vision attribution and dataset-selection application results likewise do not test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses Chinchilla-optimal token ratios and Kaplan's 6pD compute approximation as tools. Its results are correlations, across training-data distributions, between small-proxy and 760M-model losses, plus attribution LDS and dataset-selection accuracy. None of this measures how loss falls with parameters, tokens or compute. It fits no power law and estimates no compute-optimal allocation. Cross-scale prediction here concerns data effects, not loss magnitude, so it measures a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that training-data distribution generally affects small and large models similarly, even across large compute gaps. This fails for very small proxies on some tasks (SQuAD, TriviaQA). Proxies remain effective for data attribution (vision) and dataset selection (language) up to a certain relative scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares losses across training-data distributions and model scales rather than fitting held-out-loss scaling laws or estimating compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported proxy-to-reference loss correlation varies with proxy scale and test distribution; the text identifies SQuAD and TriviaQA as weaker cases for the smallest proxy.

fits_no_version.finding: Small proxies' losses correlate highly with 760M-model losses across 10 training-data distributions on most test sets. Correlation is weaker on SQuAD and TriviaQA for the smallest (370x less compute) proxy, and it rises with proxy compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How training-data choice changes LM loss is largely consistent across compute scale, with consistency degrading for very small proxies and some test tasks.

record.problems: The loss-correlation findings do not test the listed scaling-law claims. The comparisons cover a limited set of model scales and training-data distributions, and many exact correlation values are presented in figures rather than stated in the text. The main text and Appendix B differ on the small model size for Figure 1.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were included for the vision attribution and language dataset-selection applications: those measure attribution quality or selected-data downstream accuracy, not the listed loss-scaling or downstream scale-predictability versions (Sections 3.1–3.2; Figures 6 and 8).

untested.parts: The vision ResNet width sweeps report accuracy and attribution LDS, not power-law fits.
Not tested. Proxy accuracy near chance on HellaSwag/COPA concerns proxy usefulness, not predictable downstream scaling.

record.verdict_notes: There are internal inconsistencies about the Figure 1 proxy (57M/175x vs 80M/85x) and about which proxies appear in Figure 2. The paper cites Kaplan as the source for Chinchilla ratios in Section 2.1 but Hoffmann elsewhere. The vision and dataset-selection application results are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law behavior of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power laws are fitted on small runs or evaluated as predictions of larger-run loss.
No compute-budget sweep estimates loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations.
The paper does not test loss sensitivity to architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The vision experiments study attribution behavior, not whether scaling-law forms transfer to other modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports proxy-loss correlations across training-data distributions and downstream application outcomes, not predictable downstream improvement with scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitted scaling exponents or allocation laws across fitting choices, nor test for bends away from a single power law.

rows.subject: 57M proxy model vs 760M reference model
rows.operation_detail: Compared test losses across training-data distributions at two model scales.

conditions.value: Different data distributions; 10 separate distributions in the setup
Six datasets, including C4, the Pile, SQuAD, LAMBADA, HellaSwag, and TriviaQA
175× less compute for the proxy, as stated in the Figure 1 discussion

rows.measure: Correlation of proxy and reference model test losses across training-data distributions
rows.value: The losses generally highly correlate; the proxy uses 175× less compute.
rows.note: The main text identifies the proxy as 57M parameters. Appendix B.1.1 describes the Figure 1 models as MPT-80M and MPT-760M. This is a correlation across data-distribution changes, not a power-law extrapolation.
rows.check: The proxy size is inconsistent: the main text says 57M and 175x compute, while Appendix B.1.1 and Table 10 say MPT-80M (82M params, 1.67B tokens) and 85x compute. Figure R² values, about 0.65–0.99 across tasks, are only partly legible. The measure is a cross-data-distribution loss correlation, which has no bearing on any scaling-law version.

rows.subject: MPT-37M proxy model vs MPT-760M reference model
rows.operation_detail: Compared losses across training-data distributions at a larger compute gap.

conditions.value: Downstream tasks and pretraining datasets; the text identifies SQuAD and TriviaQA as weaker-correlation cases

rows.measure: Correlation of proxy and reference model losses across training-data distributions
rows.value: The text reports very strong correlation overall, slightly weaker on some tasks; it identifies SQuAD and TriviaQA as exceptions to high correlation.
rows.note: Appendix B.1.3 says the 37M model uses 0.84B tokens and the 760M model 15.9B tokens. The reported task-level correlations are primarily shown in figures.
rows.check: Figure 12 shows R² values roughly 0.46–0.99, with the low values on SQuAD and TriviaQA-type tasks. The large-model token counts are inconsistent (15.9B in Table 11 vs 15.3B elsewhere). The measure does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: MPT proxy models (125M, 220M, and 350M) vs MPT-760M reference model
rows.operation_detail: Measured loss correlation against the 760M reference at several proxy compute budgets.

conditions.value: Correlation is averaged over multiple tasks

rows.measure: Coefficient of determination between proxy and reference model losses
rows.value: The text states that correlation increases as training compute increases.
rows.note: The result is described as an average over multiple tasks; exact plotted values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: The main text says Figure 2 includes a 40M proxy, but the appendix lists only 125M, 220M and 350M. The result is that correlation rises with proxy compute, which says nothing about how loss scales.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
